first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent it, so I read it properly on the iPad, top to bottom. The first lines are about the parents being there at every stage, which got me straight away. It's calm and well mannered, and the Smartraveller line is right there in the summary. There are a lot of Japanese words to keep track of, but the paragraphs are short and I never felt lost.

journey.quote: Parents are present at every stage, from the first formal exchange of gifts to the letter a bride reads aloud at the end of the reception.
journey.reaction: Lovely. For once the parents aren't written out of it. I'm not just the chequebook here.

journey.quote: As at November 2026, Smartraveller advises Australians to "Exercise normal safety precautions" in Japan, with a higher level only for the restricted areas near the Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear power plant.
journey.reaction: Good. That's what my husband would look up first, and it's dated. It puts my mind at rest about the country itself.

journey.section: What a traditional Japanese wedding looks like today
journey.quote: Ask both families early which moments matter most to them, and build the day around those.
journey.reaction: Sensible. I'd want to speak with the groom's mother before anyone books a thing.

journey.section: 1. Yuinō: Japanese proposal traditions and the betrothal gift exchange
journey.quote: Decide early who will host, and whether relatives who cannot travel will join by video.
journey.reaction: Very practical. That's exactly the question we'd have, with my mother not able to fly far.

journey.section: 2. The Japanese wedding ceremony at a Shinto shrine
journey.quote: The ceremony is small and quiet. Close family usually attend, seated on either side of the hall, with the couple at the front before the altar.
journey.reaction: So I'd be in there. Are there chairs, or is it kneeling? Steps up to the shrine? My mother uses a walking frame. It doesn't say, and that's what I'd need to know.

journey.quote: At many weddings the parents also drink, sealing the bond between the two families.
journey.reaction: I'd like to know that before the day rather than be caught out. Glad it's spelled out.

journey.section: 4. The bride's shiromuku, iro-uchikake and the groom's hakama
journey.quote: Family members often wear their own formal kimono, the mothers in black.
journey.reaction: Oh. Am I expected to wear a black kimono? I wouldn't know where to start, or whether a dark dress would be fine. I'd have to ask, and I'd rather not feel silly asking.

journey.quote: An earlier black uchikake in its collection, worn by a merchant-class bride, probably in Kyoto, between 1800 and 1850, carries folded paper butterflies that symbolise harmony for the newly married couple.
journey.reaction: Pretty, but this is museum detail. I skimmed it to get to the practical bit.

journey.quote: Allow generous dressing time between them: a shiromuku takes far longer to put on than a gown.
journey.reaction: This is the kind of tip that saves a day from running late. I'd underline it.

journey.quote: Ask a Japanese relative or friend what is expected in your circle: the custom is personal, and families have their own sense of what is fitting.
journey.reaction: Fair, and I'd rather that than a made-up figure. Our side will be asking how much, though, so I'd want someone to help us get it right.

journey.quote: The bride stands and reads a letter to her parents, thanking them for raising her.
journey.reaction: Well, that's me in tears already. This is the part I'm sending my husband.

journey.quote: If your parents are not used to speaking in public, give them notice, and offer a translator if half the room will not follow the language.
journey.reaction: Thank you. Somebody has thought about the parents as people, not props.

journey.quote: Severe heat waves can affect Japan between July and September, and the typhoon season runs from May to November, with most activity between July and September.
journey.reaction: Heat is a real worry for older guests. And if a typhoon moves the date, what happens to our deposits? There's nothing here on transfers, getting around for someone less mobile, medical care or travel insurance.

journey.quote: Before you book, put these questions to the municipal office (the kuyakusho or shiyakusho) where you plan to marry, and to the Australian Embassy:
journey.reaction: Very useful. I'd print this. But the paperwork will be in Japanese, and I'd want to know whether anyone helps us with translation.

journey.quote: They work in your time zone and quote in AUD, the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins, and your advisor confirms the inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: That's the sentence I was looking for. Australian dollars, in writing, before any work starts. It still doesn't tell me who I ring if something goes wrong at 2am Tokyo time, or whether the supplier contracts are in English.

journey.quote: The municipal office and the Embassy set the legal steps, and the shrine or chapel sets its own.
journey.reaction: Honest about who's responsible for what, which I respect. I'd still ask whether you point us to a translator.

unanswered_questions: If we pay deposits to venues or suppliers in Japan, is that money protected, and what happens if a typhoon forces us to postpone?
Are contracts with Japanese suppliers in English, and are all quotes in Australian dollars?
Who do I ring if something goes wrong at 2am Tokyo time? Is anyone from your side there on the day?
Can an elderly guest with a walking frame manage a shrine ceremony: steps, seating, kneeling, and getting between the shrine, chapel and reception?
What travel insurance and medical cover should older guests have for Japan, especially in summer heat?
Is the mother of the bride expected to wear a black kimono, and if so, who helps with hiring and dressing?
Can you help find a certified Japanese translator for the municipal office documents?
Who is the Wedded Advisor, and can I speak to them on the phone before anything is booked?
would_share_with: My husband, with the bride's letter section, the Smartraveller line and the legal questions marked
My daughter, to ask what I'm meant to wear and whether Nana can manage the shrine

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready to talk through dates, places or a wedding at home, tell us your date, your guest list and the feeling you want, and a Wedded Advisor will start from there. Nothing is too early or too vague.
cta_reaction.why: 'Nothing is too early or too vague' is kind, and I'd feel I could ask my practical questions without looking old-fashioned. But the link at the end goes to a magazine, and I want a phone call with a real person before anything is booked. I'd click if it said that's what happens next.

top_3_changes: In the travel section, add a short note for older or less mobile guests (summer heat, shrine steps and seating, transfers between ceremony and reception, travel insurance and medical cover), written as questions to ask rather than invented details.

Next to the Wedded Advisor paragraph or the closing invitation, say plainly what happens after you get in touch (a phone call with a named person), and how postponements, deposits and English-language contracts are handled, or list them as questions to ask.
Where the mothers' black kimono is mentioned, add one line for non-Japanese parents on what they might wear and whether it's fine to ask, so a mother of the bride doesn't feel caught out.

Stayed in character as Margaret (funding parent, practical, reads top to bottom)
No invented brand facts; missing business details listed as unanswered questions
HTML comments, image slots and VERIFY markers treated as invisible
Title and deferred business details not raised as must-fix, per orchestrator

open_questions.question: Deposit protection on postponement, on-the-day support and English-language contracts remain this persona's main trust gaps, but business details are deferred. Treat as nice-to-have or route to CRO for the CTA block?
The closing section's only link is the magazine (primary). Should the closing invitation also say a phone call is the next step, for parents who want to talk before booking?

assumptions: Margaret reads the whole article on an iPad because her daughter sent it.

Persona card does not state Margaret's heritage; the black kimono reaction assumes she is the non-Japanese parent in this scenario, since the card gives her a Melbourne profile and no Japanese background.
Per orchestrator, brand voice does not discuss sourcing; the museum-detail comment is a readability point, not a request for sourcing commentary.
